solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Stuffed gun in model's bitchy facial feature

indicators.note: something stuffed has been crammed and squashed out of shape, so the letters are jumbled
'in' places the jumbled word inside the other piece

blocks.note: to model is to pose; it is the outer piece
taken as written, then scrambled

explanation.surface: A gun shoved into a catwalk model's face – with a dig at her appearance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bitchy' is a joke rather than a slur: a pug is a dog, so its face is literally canine.
explanation.definitionFit: A snub, upturned nose like a pug dog's, a canine feature, hence 'bitchy'.

clue.text: Shifty CBI enclave - Coalition destabiliser?

indicators.note: shifty letters will not stay still, so they are rearranged

blocks.note: the business lobby's initials plus a word for a pocket of territory, taken letter by letter

explanation.surface: A dodgy enclave of business bosses threatens the stability of the coalition government.
explanation.walkthrough: The CBI is the Confederation of British Industry. Vince Cable was the Lib Dem Business Secretary in the 2010 coalition, often seen as its awkward member.
explanation.definitionFit: The Liberal Democrat cabinet minister repeatedly rocked the Conservative-led coalition with outspoken remarks, so he was a likely destabiliser.

clue.text: (& 17dn.) Eye's exposé before 'Yobs': Balls has Cameron's number – personal stink

indicators.note: 'before' sets one piece in front of the next in the sequence

blocks.note: balls is slang for nonsense, as is rot
the Prime Minister lives at No. 10 Downing Street
BO is body odour
roughs are thugs or yobs

explanation.surface: Private Eye exposes Ed Balls and Cameron's household as rank – a political smear piece.
explanation.walkthrough: Ed Balls was a Labour politician, so 'Balls' reads as a name rather than nonsense. The clue's pieces are given back to front: the second word comes first in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotten Boroughs is Private Eye's long-running column exposing local-council misdeeds, so it is the magazine's exposé page.

clue.text: Email rip-off ? That's not like Brenda these days

definitions.text: That's not like Brenda these days

indicators.note: a rip-off is a fake copy, so these letters come out as a counterfeit arrangement

blocks.note: taken letter by letter

explanation.surface: A scam email is spotted, with a remark that the Queen no longer behaves that way.
explanation.walkthrough: Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for Queen Elizabeth II. Her empire is long gone, so she is no longer imperial.
explanation.definitionFit: Imperial means relating to an empire, which the British monarch no longer reigns over, hence not like her nowadays.

clue.text: Lovers tepee houses go too far

indicators.note: 'houses' means the words contain the answer within them

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A tent shared by a couple of lovers ends up taking things too far.
explanation.definitionFit: To overstep is to exceed a limit, which is going too far.

clue.text: (& 25dn.) One with DTs etc. (drunk) welcomes independent rigorous examination

indicators.note: a drunk staggers about, so the letters reel into a new order
to welcome is to take someone in, so the scrambled part takes in a letter
'with' sets one piece alongside the next

blocks.note: one as the indefinite article
taken letter by letter, then scrambled
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: An alcoholic with the shakes takes in an independent candidate – a tough test.
explanation.walkthrough: DTs are delirium tremens, the shakes of an alcoholic; the bracketed 'drunk' feeds the surface and the wordplay at once.
explanation.definitionFit: An acid test is a decisive trial, from the use of acid to prove gold genuine, so a rigorous examination.

clue.text: "Wrench to receive an honour" – hardly sincere coming from a politician

definitions.text: hardly sincere coming from a politician

indicators.note: receiving means taking something inside

blocks.note: to wrench open is to prise
Order of Merit

explanation.surface: A politician claiming it would be a wrench to accept an honour is plainly insincere.
explanation.walkthrough: PRISE takes in OM. The definition is a satirical one: a politician's promise is proverbially hollow.
explanation.definitionFit: A pledge or undertaking, which in Private Eye's cynical view means little when a politician makes it.

clue.text: PC may well be lacking the facts but giving away name

indicators.note: giving something away means losing it from the word

blocks.note: ignorant of the facts
standard abbreviation, the letter removed

explanation.surface: A dig at a police constable who may not know what's going on.
explanation.walkthrough: UNINFORMED loses one N. The surface's ignorant PC is a trap: PC is the definition's police constable in uniform.
explanation.definitionFit: A police constable typically wears a uniform, unlike a plain-clothes detective.

clue.text: Good to have a shag upside down? Then remove pants

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning it upside down reads the letters from the bottom up

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
taken as written
to bed someone is to have sex with them

explanation.surface: Advice on a bedroom romp in an unusual position, with undressing next.
explanation.walkthrough: Debag is old British public-school slang for pulling someone's trousers off as a prank; in British usage pants can also mean underwear.
explanation.definitionFit: To debag is to strip someone of their trousers, which is removing their pants in the American sense.

clue.text: Shifty, one-off, "Caviar" Blair?

indicators.note: 'off' means the unit named just before it is dropped
shifty letters will not stay still, so they are rearranged

blocks.note: one as the indefinite article, the letter removed
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dodgy one-off dig at 'Champagne Tony' Blair and his caviar-socialist lifestyle.
explanation.walkthrough: CAVIAR loses one A and the rest is rearranged. Private Eye ran 'St Albion Parish News', casting Tony Blair as the trendy vicar.
explanation.definitionFit: In Private Eye's long-running parody, Blair was the parish priest of St Albion's, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Snog Bond as required to get in restaurant?

blocks.note: to neck is to kiss passionately
a tie is a bond

explanation.surface: Does kissing James Bond count as the dress code for getting into a smart restaurant?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bond' looks like 007, but it is just a link or tie.
explanation.definitionFit: Smart restaurants once insisted on a jacket and tie, so the neckwear was required for entry.

clue.text: Blair's opening alternative Dome broadcast: it's yawn-making

definitions.note: the definition is a description; the answer is the noun for the state it causes

indicators.note: a word's opening is its first letter
broadcast seed is scattered, so these letters are scattered into a new order

blocks.note: first letter
the conjunction that offers an alternative
taken letter by letter and scrambled

explanation.surface: A Blair-era TV programme about the Millennium Dome is a real snooze.
explanation.walkthrough: The Millennium Dome was Blair's notoriously dull flagship exhibition in London for the year 2000.
explanation.definitionFit: Boredom is tedium, the weariness that makes you yawn.

clue.text: Subordinate "independent", Nick Clegg, extremely supportive

definitions.note: the answer is the -ing form, used here as an adjective

indicators.note: extremely means at the extremes, taking only the outermost letters

blocks.note: a second is an assistant or deputy
standard abbreviation
first and last letters of the name

explanation.surface: Nick Clegg, supposedly independent, is a junior partner who backs everything.
explanation.walkthrough: Clegg led the Lib Dems as Cameron's deputy in coalition, mocked as his subordinate.
explanation.definitionFit: Seconding a motion means formally backing it, so the word expresses giving support.

clue.text: In fact, Russia's a bind

indicators.note: 'in' says the answer sits inside the words that follow

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Russia, frankly, is a tricky problem.
explanation.walkthrough: The hidden name is also that of Liz Truss, a Conservative minister, which the Russian theme hints at.
explanation.definitionFit: A truss is a supporting bandage or bundle tied together, something that binds.

clue.text: Fancy nude Republican with – lord! – disgusting nether regions?

indicators.note: fancy means elaborately reworked, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
standard abbreviation
standard abbreviation
taken as written

explanation.surface: A smutty exclamation at a naked American politician exposing his unpleasant private parts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' is used twice: once as W, once in the surface. 'Nether regions' looks like the genitals; here it means the realm of the dead or of crooks.
explanation.definitionFit: The underworld is Hades, the regions below the earth, or the seedy criminal milieu, nasty either way.

clue.text: Descriptive of heated Commons debate when old Blairite female cosies up to Left?

definitions.note: the answer is a noun naming the din, not an adjective

indicators.note: cosying up to means sitting right next to, so one piece is placed beside the other

blocks.note: Blair's Babes was the press name for the women Labour MPs elected in 1997
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A former New Labour woman MP sidles up to the left wing during a rowdy Commons session.
explanation.definitionFit: Babel, from the biblical tower, is a confused uproar of many voices, which sums up a shouting match in Parliament.

clue.text: see 3dn.
Archer – using another name in Piccadilly

blocks.note: first meaning: the god of love with his bow and arrows
second meaning: the statue at Piccadilly Circus is known as Eros; this is its Roman name

explanation.surface: Jeffrey Archer is caught in Piccadilly under an alias.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeffrey Archer, the novelist peer jailed for perjury, is the false lead; the archer is the love god, called Eros at Piccadilly Circus in London.
explanation.definitionFit: Cupid is the Roman counterpart of the Greek Eros, the winged bowman of love.

clue.text: see 21ac.
Article by hack: "Pin the rap on somebody!"

blocks.note: the indefinite article
a hack is a journalist or writer

explanation.surface: A tabloid headline urging readers to blame someone, anyone.
explanation.definitionFit: To ascribe something is to attribute it to a cause or person, so to lay blame on them.

clue.text: As Cameron's PM role will turn out to be after tax involved in more dithering?

definitions.text: As Cameron's PM role will turn out to be

indicators.note: being involved in something means being caught up inside it
dithering wavers back and forth, so the letters are unsettled

blocks.note: income after tax is net
taken as written

explanation.surface: A prediction that dithering over tax will cut short Cameron's premiership.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-term leader serves a single period in office before losing power, Private Eye's forecast for Cameron.

clue.text: (& 18dn.) Lot of money invested in America (involved with an MP's dirty tricks operation)

indicators.note: money invested in something is put inside it
involved means tangled up, so the letters are mixed together

blocks.note: G is a grand, a thousand pounds or dollars
taken as written
taken letter by letter, the S included

explanation.surface: Big money poured into America, mixed up with a politician's underhand scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-S of MP's is part of the fodder, not a link. G for a grand is slang for a thousand.
explanation.definitionFit: A smear campaign is an organised effort to damage someone's reputation with innuendo, a classic dirty-tricks operation.

clue.text: Brings out the muscles and quizzes press

blocks.note: to pump someone is to question them for information
to iron clothes is to press them

explanation.surface: Someone shows off their muscles and grills the journalists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'press' looks like the newspapers but is the verb for smoothing clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Pumping iron is weightlifting, which builds up and displays the muscles.

clue.text: Bribe taken up: Miliband was affected?

indicators.note: in a down entry, taken up means read from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: a sop is a small bribe to placate someone
Ed Miliband, Labour leader

explanation.surface: Was Ed Miliband swayed after accepting a bribe?
explanation.walkthrough: 'affected' seems to mean influenced, but here it means putting on airs.
explanation.definitionFit: To pose is to behave affectedly, striking an attitude for effect.

clue.text: Prickteaser Monica delivers lecture

indicators.note: to deliver is to bring forth from within, so the answer emerges from inside the words

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Monica, the flirt, gives a talk – an allusion to Monica Lewinsky and Bill Clinton.
explanation.definitionFit: A sermon is a moralising talk, so a lecture.

clue.text: They're taken to avoid congestion when shopper gets diarrhoea

blocks.note: a shopper is an informer, one who shops others to the police, as a rat does
the runs is slang for diarrhoea

explanation.surface: Someone out shopping gets an upset stomach – a different kind of congestion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shopper' looks like someone at the supermarket; in British slang to shop someone is to inform on them.
explanation.definitionFit: Rat runs are side streets drivers use as shortcuts to dodge traffic jams on main roads.

clue.text: see 6dn.
Maybe John Lennon's manner with drink

blocks.note: an air is a manner or bearing
port is a fortified wine

explanation.surface: The late Beatle's style, combined with a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Liverpool's airport is named Liverpool John Lennon Airport; the surface wants the musician.
explanation.definitionFit: Liverpool John Lennon Airport is one example of an aerodrome named after a famous person.

clue.text: Artist representing London mayor ("King and Emperor not allowed") with his short office accessory

indicators.note: what is not allowed is kept out, so those letters are left out

blocks.note: Boris Johnson, then Mayor of London
R for rex, king, and I for imperator, emperor; these are removed
a mayor wears a chain of office; ch. is the abbreviation for chain

explanation.surface: Boris Johnson, denied grand titles, makes do with a small piece of office kit.
explanation.walkthrough: Hieronymus Bosch was the Dutch painter of nightmarish scenes. 'Office accessory' suggests a stapler, but it is the mayoral chain.
explanation.definitionFit: Bosch was an early Netherlandish painter, an artist known for The Garden of Earthly Delights.

clue.text: God-awful Nick's pious habit

indicators.note: something awful is a mess, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written and scrambled
to nick and to collar both mean to arrest

explanation.surface: Nick Clegg's dreadful habit of piety, with an oath thrown in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' reads as Clegg, but nick is British slang for arrest.
explanation.definitionFit: A clerical collar is part of a priest's dress, and habit here means religious clothing.
